questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{1}[t],$ the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most $1,$ and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1).
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=5t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=-2t+2,\,q(t)=-t-4
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t)\}$ equals $-5t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t)={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)=-5t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{p}_{2}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t)=\frac{⟨q(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{p}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨q(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =q(0){p}_{2}(0)+q(1){p}_{2}(1) \\  & =(-t-4){|}_{0}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{0}+(-t-4){|}_{1}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{1} \\  & =(-4)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 0 \\  & =-8,\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={p}_{2}(0){p}_{2}(0)+{p}_{2}(1){p}_{2}(1) \\  & =(-2t+2)^{2}{|}_{0}+(-2t+2)^{2}{|}_{1} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) & =\frac{-8}{4}\cdot (-2t+2)=4t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) \\  & =-5t+(4t-4) \\  & =-t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{1}[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $1$ with real coefficients. Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=4t$ and $g(t)=3t-3$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The distance between $f(t)=4t$ and $g(t)=3t-3$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖4t-(3t-3)‖ \\  & =‖t+3‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨t+3,t+3⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨t+3,t+3⟩ & =(t+3){|}_{0}\cdot (t+3){|}_{0}+(t+3){|}_{1}\cdot (t+3){|}_{1} \\  & =3\cdot 3+4\cdot 4 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{25}=5.$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=8t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=4t-2$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $f(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{g(t)\}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t) & =\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}8t\cdot (4t-2)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(4t-2)^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}(32{t}^{2}-16t)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(16{t}^{2}-16t+4)\,\text{d}t}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{[\frac{32}{3}{t}^{3}-8{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1}}{[\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}-8{t}^{2}+4t]_{0}^{1}}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{(\frac{32}{3}-8)-0}{(\frac{16}{3}-4)-0}\cdot (6t-3) \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8}{3})}{(\frac{4}{3})}\cdot (4t+2) \\  & =2\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =8t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The distance between $f(t)=8t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=4t-2$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t)‖ \\  & =‖8t-(8t-4)‖ \\  & =‖4‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨4,4⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨4,4⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}16\,\text{d}t \\  & =16t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =16-0 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{16}=4.$
